_README: The year-ahead panel, as data instead of code. One object per condition. price_row_id points at a row that is already in prices.json, so no figure lives here and nothing new is asserted; the panel renders whatever that row says, with that row's year, population and coverage statement. A condition with price_row_id null renders the absence and sends the person to /gap so the gap is COUNTED rather than filled. Adding a condition is one object — but only after its figure exists as a verified row in prices.json.
_the_distinction_that_must_stay_on_the_f: These figures are not the same KIND of number and must never be ranked against each other as if they were. An EXCESS figure is what a person spends OVER a comparable person who does not have the condition — the care the condition added. A CONDITION-ATTRIBUTED figure is what was spent on treating that condition, and it excludes everything else the person spent. figure_kind carries which one it is, and the panel prints it.

conditions.label: Long COVID
conditions.icd10cm_source: CDC/NCHS, ICD-10-CM code descriptions, FY2026 and FY2027
conditions.figure_kind_label: the EXTRA a person spends in a year, over a comparable adult who never had COVID
conditions.note: The published figure is an interval, and the interval is the answer. It is not what long COVID costs — it is what a year of it added, after adjusting for age, income, insurance and other conditions.
conditions.definition_caveat: Long COVID here is self-reported — the person said yes to having had COVID and yes to symptoms lasting three months or more. It is not a U09.9 diagnosis, so it includes people who never got one.
conditions.icd10cm_billable_note: A code that may be submitted on a claim.
conditions.icd10cm_first_effective_evidence: absent from the FY2021 file, present in the FY2022 file
conditions.figure_publisher_note: A peer-reviewed secondary analysis of the federal survey, not a federal publication. The data underneath is AHRQ MEPS 2022; the estimate is the authors’, and we say so wherever we print it.

conditions.label: Heart disease
conditions.figure_kind_label: what was spent TREATING this condition in a year, per adult being treated for it
conditions.note: Here as a yardstick. A named, visible, well-funded chronic condition costs about the same per year as the excess attributable to long COVID.
conditions.definition_caveat: The mean is more than seven times the median for the same population ($660). Most people treated for heart disease spend far less than the mean; a few spend enormously more.
conditions.icd10cm_blank_reason: AHRQ MEPS Statistical Brief #562 prices adults TREATED FOR HEART DISEASE, a clinical category that spans the whole I00-I99 circulatory chapter. No single ICD-10-CM code names that population, so this row carries none.
conditions.figure_publisher_note: Published by AHRQ, the federal agency that runs the survey.

conditions.label: Diabetes
conditions.figure_kind_label: what was spent TREATING this condition in a year, per adult being treated for it
conditions.note: A second yardstick. Four fifths of it is prescription drugs — which is exactly why a condition with no approved drug therapy can devastate someone and still measure smaller.
conditions.definition_caveat: AHRQ states these estimates exclude lost productivity and exclude complication care such as related emergency and hospital use, so they are not comparable to broader cost-of-illness estimates.
conditions.icd10cm_blank_reason: AHRQ MEPS Statistical Brief #568 prices adults TREATED FOR DIABETES, which spans E08 through E13. E11 alone is type 2 only, so no single code names the population the $5,810 came from.
conditions.figure_publisher_note: Published by AHRQ, the federal agency that runs the survey.

conditions.label: Still looking for a diagnosis
conditions.note: There is no federal figure for a year spent looking. That is the gap this tool exists to count — the visits and tests below are priced, the search itself is not.
conditions.icd10cm_blank_reason: There is no ICD-10-CM code for not yet having a diagnosis. R69, "Illness, unspecified", is a code for an unspecified illness, not for a search; using it here would put a diagnosis on someone who does not have one.

_when_there_is_no_figure: We have not found a published federal annual figure for this condition. That is a statement about what we could find, not a claim that none exists anywhere — if you know of one, say so and we will price it and cite it.

_icd10cm_source.what: Every ICD-10-CM code below was re-read in the code-description file CDC/NCHS publishes for the fiscal year, not typed from memory. The browser a clinician would use is the same data: https://icd10cmtool.cdc.gov/ (NCHS ICD-10-CM Web Application, multi-year edition).
_icd10cm_source.field_read: icd10cm-order-<FY>.txt, columns: order number, code, 1 if the code may be submitted on a claim / 0 if it is a category heading, short description, long description. The long description is what we print.
_icd10cm_source.why_two_years: The FY2027 code set takes effect on 1 October 2026. Every code here is present, billable-or-heading identical, and titled identically in both files, so nothing on this page changes when the code set turns over.
_icd10cm_source.first_effective_method: A first-effective date is asserted only where the code is ABSENT from an earlier year file and PRESENT in the year claimed. The earlier files read are FY2021 (icd10cm-codes-order-Jan-2021.zip, sha256 dffa100f5bc7e588cca63257c0da0668094b31ba9812283eba893d082d2e909f), FY2022 (2022/Code Descriptions zip.zip, sha256 bab2b3b041cf4b999f8380f3198c1dd6ca404ba7d5513ec60efc813a97f7c214) and FY2023 (icd10-Order-CodeFiles2023.zip, sha256 a7bfd4511dc154bff96fe0ced5fcd633bd26f997ccd6ae386f5c24595e1789b5). Where a code predates every file we read, we say that instead of inventing a date.

_no_code_is_not_an_oversight: Some rows here carry no ICD-10-CM code on purpose, and the count is printed from the data rather than written into the prose. AHRQ MEPS prices a CLINICAL CATEGORY ("adults treated for heart disease", "adults treated for diabetes"), which spans dozens of codes; picking one code to stand for it would misdescribe the population the figure came from. And there is no code for not yet having a diagnosis. A blank we can explain beats a code we cannot defend.
